title: Accuweather Meteorologist teaches Sydni and Alyssa about the Orionid Meteor Shower
excerpt: Wednesday night through early Thursday debris from Halley’s Comet will leave traces of stardust across the night sky.
content:
ROCKFORD, Ill. (Rockford News First) - Wednesday night through early Thursday debris from Halley’s Comet will leave traces of stardust across the night sky.

AccuWeather senior meteorologist Tom Kynes says the Orionid Meteor Shower, may not be the most impressive one, but it’s still a sight to see.

“We can expect anywhere from 10 to 20 meteors per hour,” he predicts. “If we’re lucky, we’ll get to see some long trails from these meteors across the sky as well.”

In the Northern Illinois region, Kines says the weather outlook looks pretty good for viewing, especially after midnight.

“We’re watching a few patchy clouds that are moving east out of Iowa and a little bit of cloudiness. moving south across Wisconsin, which could be an issue early on, but later tonight, which is the best viewing anyway for these meteors, it’s looking pretty good.”

However, he says you might have to deal with a bit of patchy fog very late tonight.

“I think in general, once we get past 10 P.m. or so, it’s looking pretty good,” said Kines. “It is close to a full moon tonight. which obviously causes problems. The moon sets shortly after midnight tonight. So again, the latter part of the night looks like the best part of the night for viewing.”

What makes the Orionid Meteor Shower special is that it is known for producing some long trails across the sky. Not all the meteor showers do that.

“Your best bet is to get away from the urban city lights, get out in the rural areas. You have to have your eyes adjust to the darkness. So, you got to stay out in the dark for 15, 20 minutes or so, your eyes can adjust,” Kines advises. And that means turning the phone off. If you’re outside in your yard, turn the outside lights off. No flashlights."

Kines adds your best viewing is toward the east. He says you might see four or five right away, followed by a long lull where you don’t see one. Just be patient, Kines says, it’s coming.
